title: Upland Geopolitics
abstract: Winner of the 2024 EuroSEAS Social Science Book Prize Cold War legacies in Southeast Asia enable new geographies of enclosure In the twenty-first century, land deals in the Global South have become increasingly prevalent and controversial. Transnational access to arable land in impoverished "land-rich" countries in Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia highlights the link between the shifting geopolitics of economic development and problems of food security, climate change, and regional and international trade. Drawing on ethnographic and archival research, Upland Geopolitics uses the case of Chinese agribusiness investment in northern Laos to study the unbalanced geography of the new global land rush. Connecting the current rubber plantation boom to a longer trajectory of foreign intervention in the region, Upland Geopolitics reveals how legacies of Cold War conflict continue to pave the way for transnational enclosure in a socially uneven landscape. Upland Geopolitics is freely available in an open access edition thanks to TOME (Toward an Open Monograph Ecosystem) and the generous support of Indiana University. DOI: 10.6069/9780295750507

narrative:
Short impact summary

Upland Geopolitics (2022), published by University of Washington Press, has been cited 17 times — enough that OpenAlex puts it in the top 10% of works in its field and year. Beyond that, it is used in teaching.

Full narrative

Upland Geopolitics by Michael B. Dwyer was published by University of Washington Press in 2022. Conceptually, the work connects to Geopolitics, Geography, Political science, Politics and Law. The book was recognised: ACLS Open Access Book Prize & Arcadia Open Access Publishing Award finalist (2026) — Anthropology.

OpenAlex records 17 citations. That places it in the top 10% of works in its field and year of publication. Citations peaked in 2025 with 15 citing works. Notable citing venues include The Journal of Peasant Studies, Globalizations and Development and Change. The citing works include 16 journal articles and 1 book. They come from 14 countries, led by the United States, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom.

In teaching, it is discussed in 2 recorded lectures. It has been downloaded 88 times via Ubiquity Press.
narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

Upland Geopolitics has already shown clear scholarly uptake, with 17 OpenAlex citations and a field-normalized standing in the top 10% for its year. The record also shows early educational use through two recorded book talks, alongside 88 tracked downloads, suggesting the book is finding both academic and teaching audiences.

Full narrative

Michael B. Dwyer’s Upland Geopolitics is receiving focused attention in the literature on land, agrarian change, and Southeast Asian political economy. The book’s citation profile is concentrated in relevant journals, especially The Journal of Peasant Studies and Globalizations, indicating that researchers are engaging it as part of active debates on land rushes, dispossession, territorial governance, and the politics of development. Its top concepts in the citing landscape align closely with the book’s own themes, particularly agriculture and land use, land rights and reforms, and Southeast Asian sociopolitical studies.

The citation record is also geographically and thematically broad within that specialist area. Recent citing works span comparative studies of land rushes and agrarian change in places including Paraguay, Laos, Cambodia, Myanmar, and Colombia, showing that the book is being used as a reference point beyond its core case of postwar Laos. This pattern suggests conceptual influence: the book appears to be helping frame how scholars think about enclosure, territorial transformation, and the political economy of land across different regional settings.

Beyond citations, the book has visible signs of teaching and public scholarly discussion. Two recorded book talks, hosted by UBC School of Public Policy and Global Affairs and SOAS University of London, indicate that the work has been presented in educational settings. The book is also openly accessible in hybrid form and has 88 recorded downloads, which points to direct readership and ease of access rather than solely citation-based impact.

The wider record remains relatively early and selective, so the clearest story is one of emerging but already well-targeted scholarly influence. The book has a strong citation base for its age, recognized field standing, and measurable circulation through open-access channels. Taken together, these signals show a monograph that is being taken up where its arguments are most relevant: in ongoing research on land governance, agrarian change, and the geopolitics of development in the Global South.
